Where lockout signs go

  • At main disconnects and every energy isolation point.
  • On machines with more than one energy source: electric, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity or stored pressure.
  • At the lockout station where locks and tags are kept.
  • Where workers clear jams, clean, change blades or reach into the machine.

What the standard requires

OSHA 1910.147 requires written energy control procedures, training and periodic inspections. Tags must warn against hazardous conditions with a legend such as Do Not Start, Do Not Open, Do Not Close, Do Not Energize or Do Not Operate. A sign at the equipment reminds people that the procedure applies and where the isolation points are. It does not replace locks, tags or the written procedure.

Common questions

Is a sign the same as a lockout tag?

No. A tag goes on the isolating device during service. A sign is a permanent reminder at the equipment. Most programs use both.

Can you put our machine number or isolation points on a sign?

Yes. Custom signs are priced close to catalog signs.

Where to post

  • Roof access doors and hatches, and along roof edges.
  • Floor and roof openings and skylights.
  • Open-sided platforms, mezzanine gates and dock edges.
  • Anchor points and fall protection gear stations.
  • Ladder and scaffold access points.

Standards to know

In general industry, OSHA 1910.28 requires fall protection at 4 feet and covers holes, skylights and open-sided floors. In construction, 1926.501 sets the trigger at 6 feet. Signs mark the edge and remind people to tie off. They support guardrails, covers and personal fall arrest systems, not replace them.

Common questions

Can a sign be used instead of a guardrail?

No. Use signs to mark the hazard and the rule, along with the physical protection the standard calls for.

Do you make roof access signs?

Yes. Roof edge, skylight and tie-off signs are in this collection, and the roof kits bundle them.
